Overview: Why training data matters for hallucination control in abstractive summarization
- Abstractive summarization models frequently hallucinate content that is unsupported or contradictory relative to the source; these errors fall into intrinsic (contradictions or coreference errors tied to the input) and extrinsic (novel content not inferable from the input) categories, with human evaluations showing that most summaries contain hallucinations and many extrinsic hallucinations are erroneous rather than factual <cite id="48615a0b-0">Intrinsic and extrinsic hallucinations happen frequently -in more than 70% of single-sentence summaries, with over 90% of extrinsic hallucinations being erroneous</cite> <cite id="48615a0b-3">An abstract summary is hallucinated if it contains any span not semantically supported by the input; intrinsic hallucinations are contradictions with the input, while extrinsic hallucinations are unsupported spans</cite> <cite id="48615a0b-4">Neural abstractive summarization models often hallucinate; even with hallucinations, high ROUGE is possible, motivating faithfulness-focused evaluation</cite>.
- Training data shapes what the model learns as “acceptable abstraction,” and noisy or overly abstractive references, as well as human-written summaries with extrinsic content, can bias models to hallucinate during fine-tuning <cite id="107608e7-1">Human ground-truth summaries can contain information not present in inputs; training on such data may increase hallucination; attention to irrelevant context and noncontextual knowledge also drive errors</cite> <cite id="107608e7-3">Extrinsic hallucinations arise from ignoring the source; early correction is crucial to avoid error propagation</cite> <cite id="48615a0b-3">Extrinsic hallucinations can arise from human-written summaries that the model overfits during training</cite> <cite id="e43d4e65-3">Creating extractive labels from abstractive references can be inaccurate for highly abstract references; filtering overly abstractive references improves training and evaluation</cite>.

Data-centric levers to reduce hallucinations

1) Curate and filter the training set to remove sources of extrinsic noise
- Remove or downweight examples where references are overly abstractive or misaligned with the source; such cases teach spurious abstraction and degrade faithfulness <cite id="e43d4e65-3">Filtering references with zero bigram overlap from the document reduces noisy training signals; filtering improved results on CNN/DM and Newsroom</cite>.
- Guard against “data-driven semantic drift”: when training data includes summaries with unsupported additions, models learn to hallucinate; prefer references grounded by extractive signals or human-checked summaries, and use automatic tools to flag unsupported entities/quantities before training <cite id="107608e7-1">Training on summaries that include non-present information can increase hallucination; extrinsic hallucinations can stem from human-written summaries</cite> <cite id="48615a0b-4">A verification system for non-factual quantities plus re-ranking reduced hallucinated quantities in outputs</cite>.
- Practical pipeline: pair documents with multiple human references, compute overlap-based grounding, drop or correct misaligned spans; optionally rank reference summaries by semantic support before fine-tuning <cite id="e43d4e65-3">Overlap-based filtering of overly abstractive references yields cleaner training sets and better downstream results</cite>.

2) Add faithfulness-aware supervision signals during training
- Mine unfaithful spans and use them as negative examples: training with gradient ascent, unlikelihood training, or task vector negation on annotated unfaithful spans improves faithfulness; unlikelihood and task vector negation were most effective in ablation <cite id="48615a0b-1">Span-level hallucination annotations enable fine-tuning via gradient ascent, unlikelihood training, and task vector negation; unlikelihood and task vector negation improved faithfulness, with stable gains across weighting schedules</cite>.
- Reference-grounded fact consistency: leverage reference summaries as positives and generate erroneous summaries as negatives to train discriminators that distinguish faithful from unfaithful outputs, directly penalizing unsupported facts <cite id="48615a0b-1">Using unfaithful spans mined from reference-grounded data improves faithfulness</cite> <cite id="e43d4e65-4">Train with reference summaries as positive data and erroneous summaries as negatives to improve fact consistency</cite>.
- Entity-level verification and re-ranking: teach models to avoid hallucinated entities by incorporating entity classification/verification objectives and re-ranking steps to reduce hallucinated quantities; these auxiliary signals improve entity-level factuality without harming abstractiveness <cite id="48615a0b-4">Entity classification as auxiliary objective improves entity-level factuality; verification and re-ranking reduce hallucinated quantities in outputs</cite>.
- Reinforcement learning signals from faithfulness metrics or detectors: RL-based objectives and preference optimization can improve faithfulness, but risk overfitting to chosen signals if not balanced with generalization tasks; FactPegasus-style contrastive setups combining ROUGE and FactCC can help, yet degrade overall summarization if over-optimized <cite id="48615a0b-1">FactPegasus combines ROUGE and FactCC in contrastive pretraining to boost faithfulness, but risks overfitting to metrics</cite> <cite id="48615a0b-2">RL-based objectives have been used to enhance faithfulness; decoding strategies (ITI, DoLa, lookahead) can improve faithfulness but do not change the model’s parameters</cite>.

3) Design training data and pretraining corpora to encode faithfulness and semantic coherence
- Faithfulness-constrained pretraining: pretraining with objectives that encourage semantic coherence and faithfulness, even when training on unlabeled data, improves downstream low-shot generalization; adding explicit faithfulness constraints during pretraining yields more concise, coherent, and faithful abstractive summaries <cite id="e43d4e65-0">PELMS pretraining uses semantic coherence heuristics and faithfulness constraints over a 93M-document, 3M-cluster multi-document corpus; in low-shot multi-document summarization, it improves informativeness, abstractiveness, coherence, and faithfulness</cite>.
- Large-scale unlabeled corpora for language modeling: leveraging massive unlabeled text to pretrain encoders/decoders enhances summarization quality, but faithfulness must be explicitly enforced via semantic matching or entailment signals; otherwise models prefer abstraction that introduces unsupported content <cite id="e43d4e65-4">Pretraining encoder-decoder models on large unlabeled corpora improves generation; faithfulness requires modeling facts in the source and using faithfulness evaluation as a direct signal</cite>.
- Multi-document training sets with cluster-based diversity: topic-centric clusters provide broader coverage of entities and facts, improving the ability to abstain from unsupported content and promoting faithful fusion rather than copying <cite id="e43d4e65-0">A multi-document pre-training corpus with 93M documents and 3M topic-centric clusters supports training models that generate faithful summaries across genres</cite> <cite id="e43d4e65-1">Extending encoder-decoder to multi-document settings is challenging due to scarce labeled data; pointer-generator mechanisms copy from sources and fuse sentences</cite>.

4) Train extractive–abstractive hybrids and selectors to maintain grounded abstraction
- Copying mechanisms: pointer-generator networks explicitly copy source words/phrases, which increases faithfulness but reduces abstractiveness; careful training and selection can balance the two <cite id="e43d4e65-1">Pointer-generator networks enable copying from source text and sentence fusion; this supports moving from single- to multi-document summarization</cite> <cite id="48615a0b-2">FactPegasus modifies sentence selection by combining ROUGE with FactCC to favor grounded content over hallucinated abstractions</cite>.
- Control abstractiveness to match ground truth: models that generate more unigrams/bigrams/trigrams absent from the source increase hallucination risk; training with constraints or selecting for realistic abstractiveness levels improves fidelity to reference summaries <cite id="107608e7-2">Measuring abstractiveness as the fraction of n-grams in the summary but not the source reveals that high abstractiveness correlates with hallucinations; training can reduce this gap to approach reference levels</cite>.
- Evaluate “effective faithfulness” to separate gains from extractiveness: train selectors that enforce extractiveness-aware baselines to measure improvements that are not merely from copying more content; this reveals that many advances stem from increased extractiveness and motivates methods that raise abstraction while preserving faithfulness <cite id="e43d4e65-2">Effective faithfulness isolates faithfulness gains independent of extractiveness; analysis shows improved faithfulness often comes from higher extractiveness, motivating models that are both more abstractive and more faithful</cite>.

Practical pipelines: detecting, filtering, and selecting with faithfulness signals
- Use semantic-inference metrics (e.g., BERTScore-style, FactCC) and human-in-the-loop checks to triage training sets: models trained with such signals produce more faithful outputs than ROUGE-only training; intrinsic contradictions can be detected by fact consistency models, while extrinsic unsupported spans require semantic overlap checks <cite id="48615a0b-0">Semantic inference-based automatic measures better capture faithfulness/factuality than ROUGE/BERTScore</cite> <cite id="48615a0b-2">FactPegasus uses ROUGE+FactCC to guide contrastive pretraining; overfitting to metrics can degrade general quality</cite> <cite id="107608e7-1">Models may hallucinate by attending to irrelevant context or using noncontextual knowledge; training data with extrinsic content amplifies this</cite>.
- Build iterative selection loops: train extractive baselines to produce candidate references, filter out misaligned/overly abstractive spans, run entity/quantity verification, and re-rank summaries to reduce hallucinations before using them for abstractive fine-tuning <cite id="e43d4e65-3">Overlap-based filtering of overly abstractive references improves training sets; extractive labels derived from references can be tuned to avoid noisy supervision</cite> <cite id="48615a0b-4">Verification and re-ranking reduced hallucinated quantities in final summaries</cite>.
- Combine span-level unfaithful mining with RLHF-style preference optimization: label hallucinated spans on held-out verification sets, then fine-tune abstractive models to disfavor those patterns; this improves faithfulness without catastrophic drops in ROUGE when balanced correctly <cite id="48615a0b-1">Span-level unfaithful mining via unlikelihood training and task vector negation improves faithfulness</cite> <cite id="48615a0b-2">RL-based objectives can enhance faithfulness; decoding-time interventions alone don’t change model parameters</cite>.

Mechanisms and trade-offs to manage
- Source-grounded decoding vs. knowledge-driven abstraction: intrinsic hallucinations benefit from mechanisms that enforce semantic matching to the source; extrinsic hallucinations reflect reliance on external knowledge; retrieval-augmented training data and reference-grounded objectives mitigate both types by constraining generation to supported content <cite id="107608e7-1">Attending to irrelevant context or external knowledge contributes to hallucinations; training data content strongly influences hallucination rates</cite> <cite id="107608e7-3">Extrinsic hallucinations arise from ignoring the source; early correction is crucial</cite>.
- Abstractiveness–faithfulness trade-off: naive pursuit of ROUGE often increases abstractiveness at the cost of faithfulness; constrained pretraining, extractive copying, and extractiveness-aware selectors can raise faithfulness while approaching reference-level abstraction <cite id="48615a0b-2">FactPegasus modifies sentence selection to prefer grounded content, reducing hallucinations</cite> <cite id="107608e7-2">High abstractiveness measured by n-gram absence from the source indicates hallucinations; training can reduce abstractiveness gap to ground-truth levels</cite> <cite id="e43d4e65-2">Effective faithfulness analysis shows many faithfulness gains stem from higher extractiveness, motivating methods that improve both</cite>.
- Risks of metric overfitting and sampling: optimizing solely against faithfulness metrics or heavy use of sampling can hurt generalization or overfit to artifacts; balanced multi-objective training, diverse pretraining corpora, and robust validation with semantic inference metrics reduce these risks <cite id="48615a0b-2">Overfitting to FactCC/ROUGE can degrade overall summarization quality; RL-based objectives require careful design</cite> <cite id="48615a0b-4">High ROUGE can coexist with hallucinations, necessitating faithfulness-aware evaluation and training</cite>.

Actionable checklist: improving training data to prevent hallucinations
- Curate references: drop misaligned/overly abstractive references; prefer human-checked or extractive-grounded references; rank references by semantic support before training <cite id="e43d4e65-3">Filtering references with no bigram overlap improves training and yields better scores</cite> <cite id="107608e7-1">Training on summaries with extrinsic content increases hallucination risk</cite>.
- Add faithfulness supervision: mine unfaithful spans and include them as hard negatives; train with unlikelihood or task vector negation; build positive/negative pairs using references and generated errors <cite id="48615a0b-1">Unlikelihood and task vector negation on span-level unfaithful data improve faithfulness</cite> <cite id="e43d4e65-4">Use reference summaries as positives and erroneous summaries as negatives to train better fact consistency</cite>.
- Use entity/quantity verification: incorporate entity classification/verification and re-ranking to reduce hallucinated entities/quantities before or during fine-tuning <cite id="48615a0b-4">Entity classification plus verification and re-ranking reduced hallucinated quantities</cite>.
- Enforce grounded abstraction: add copy-based objectives and semantic coherence/entailment signals; pretrain on large, diverse corpora with faithfulness constraints; in low-resource or multi-document settings, use cluster-based pretraining to improve faithfulness at low shot <cite id="e43d4e65-0">Faithfulness-constrained pretraining on multi-document clusters improves informativeness, abstractiveness, coherence, and faithfulness at minimal fine-tuning</cite> <cite id="e43d4e65-1">Pointer-generator and MMR adaptation help extend to multi-document summarization with scarce labels</cite>.
- Balance abstractiveness: train selectors to match reference-level abstractiveness and measure effective faithfulness to ensure abstraction gains don’t come from copying more unsupported content <cite id="107608e7-2">Controlling abstractiveness to approach ground-truth reduces hallucinations</cite> <cite id="e43d4e65-2">Effective faithfulness isolates gains beyond extractiveness</cite>.
- Validate with faithfulness metrics: include semantic inference-based metrics and human evaluations in selection loops; avoid ROUGE-only optimization to prevent undetected hallucinations <cite id="48615a0b-0">Semantic inference-based measures better approximate true faithfulness than ROUGE/BERTScore</cite>.

Takeaway
- Hallucinations in abstractive summarization arise from training on noisy, misaligned, or overly abstract references and from generating unsupported content; targeted data curation, faithfulness-aware supervision, and faithfulness-constrained pretraining consistently reduce hallucinations while preserving abstractiveness when balanced with extractive grounding and entity-level verification <cite id="107608e7-1">Human-written summaries with extrinsic content bias models to hallucinate</cite> <cite id="48615a0b-1">Span-level unfaithful mining via unlikelihood and task vector negation improves faithfulness</cite> <cite id="e43d4e65-0">Faithfulness-constrained pretraining on diverse multi-document corpora yields faithful summarization without excessive fine-tuning</cite> <cite id="48615a0b-4">Entity verification and re-ranking reduce hallucinated quantities and improve entity factuality</cite>. These interventions are more effective than decoding-only tricks, which do not alter underlying learned biases, underscoring that improving training data and supervision is central to preventing hallucinations in abstractive summarization <cite id="48615a0b-2">Decoding strategies improve faithfulness but do not change the model; RL-based objectives and metric-guided training can improve faithfulness but risk overfitting</cite>.

Title: Enhancing Faithfulness in Abstractive Summarization via Span-Level Fine-Tuning
Snippet: In this study, we propose leveraging span-level hallucination annotations to improve the faithfulness of LLM-generated summaries. To this end, we construct a dataset containing organically generated summaries labeled at the span level and evaluate three fine-tuning methods-gradient ascent, unlikelihood training, and task vector negation-that leverage unfaithful summary spans. Our results show that all three approaches improve summarization faithfulness, with unlikelihood training and task vector negation being more effective. Additionally, we analyze the impact of varying the weight of negative samples (ϵ) and find that unlikelihood training remains the most stable across a wide range of values. These findings highlight the effectiveness of span-level annotations in mitigating hallucinations and offer insights into robust fine-tuning strategies for improving LLM faithfulness.

Title: Model-based Preference Optimization in Abstractive Summarization without Human Feedback
Snippet: In the realm of auto-regressive language models, there are two primary approaches aimed to enhance the model's summarization capabilities: adjusting the learning algorithm or refining the decoding strategy (Welleck et al., 2020b). Decoding Strategies Several methods have been proposed to rectify hallucinations during generation. Inference-time intervention (ITI) shifts activations along truth-correlated directions (Li et al., 2023), repeating the same intervention autoregressively until the entire answer is generated. 

Decoding by contrasting layers (DoLa) uses an early-exit strategy by contrasting the differences in logits obtained from projecting the later layers versus earlier layers (Chuang et al., 2023). Learning Algorithms To mitigate hallucinations, naively fine-tuning with faithfulness-aware objectives might seem straightforward. Snippet: We adopt the definition of hallucination for abstractive summarization from Maynez et al. (2020a): 

The summary S for a context document C contains hallucinations if there exists a span in S which is not supported by C. 

Hallucinations exhibit task-specific characteristics in various Natural Language Generation (NLG) tasks. For instance, in Machine Translation, hallucination is often observed in the output when the input source undergoes specific perturbation (Lee et al., 2018). In Question Answering (QA), one common manifestation is semantic drift, where the generated answers deviate from the topic of the question (Li et al., 2021). Additionally, in retrievalbased QA, the retrieval model may introduce additional sources of hallucination (Ji et al., 2023). 

Various existing works seek to understand how hallucination happens, and have identified several factors. In various datasets, human generated ground truth summaries can contain additional information not present in the corresponding input texts (Dhingra et al., 2019;Wang et al., 2020). Training on such data may increase a model's tendency to hallucinate. During generation, hallucination may occur when the model attends to irrelevant parts of the input context (Tian et al., 2019), or utilizes knowledge acquired during training that is not grounded in the context (Longpre et al., 2021). Additionally, the decoding method also impacts the faithfulness of generation. Past work has observed that sampling-based decoding can lead to increased hallucination (Dziri et al., 2021;Lee et al., 2022;Wan et al., 2023).

Title: PELMS: Pre-training for Effective Low-Shot Multi-Document Summarization
Snippet: We investigate pre-training techniques for abstractive multi-document summarization (MDS), which is much less studied than summarizing single documents. Though recent work has demonstrated the effectiveness of highlighting information salience for pre-training strategy design, they struggle to generate abstractive and reflective summaries, which are critical properties for MDS. Overview: Why training data matters for hallucination control in abstractive summarization
- Abstractive summarization models frequently hallucinate content that is unsupported or contradictory relative to the source; these errors fall into intrinsic (contradictions or coreference errors tied to the input) and extrinsic (novel content not inferable from the input) categories, with human evaluations showing that most summaries contain hallucinations and many extrinsic hallucinations are erroneous rather than factual <cite id="48615a0b-0">Intrinsic and extrinsic hallucinations happen frequently -in more than 70% of single-sentence summaries, with over 90% of extrinsic hallucinations being erroneous</cite> <cite id="48615a0b-3">An abstract summary is hallucinated if it contains any span not semantically supported by the input; intrinsic hallucinations are contradictions with the input, while extrinsic hallucinations are unsupported spans</cite> <cite id="48615a0b-4">Neural abstractive summarization models often hallucinate; even with hallucinations, high ROUGE is possible, motivating faithfulness-focused evaluation</cite>.
- Training data shapes what the model learns as “acceptable abstraction,” and noisy or overly abstractive references, as well as human-written summaries with extrinsic content, can bias models to hallucinate during fine-tuning <cite id="107608e7-1">Human ground-truth summaries can contain information not present in inputs; training on such data may increase hallucination; attention to irrelevant context and noncontextual knowledge also drive errors</cite> <cite id="107608e7-3">Extrinsic hallucinations arise from ignoring the source; early correction is crucial to avoid error propagation</cite> <cite id="48615a0b-3">Extrinsic hallucinations can arise from human-written summaries that the model overfits during training</cite> <cite id="e43d4e65-3">Creating extractive labels from abstractive references can be inaccurate for highly abstract references; filtering overly abstractive references improves training and evaluation</cite>.

Data-centric levers to reduce hallucinations

1) Curate and filter the training set to remove sources of extrinsic noise
- Remove or downweight examples where references are overly abstractive or misaligned with the source; such cases teach spurious abstraction and degrade faithfulness <cite id="e43d4e65-3">Filtering references with zero bigram overlap from the document reduces noisy training signals; filtering improved results on CNN/DM and Newsroom</cite>.
- Guard against “data-driven semantic drift”: when training data includes summaries with unsupported additions, models learn to hallucinate; prefer references grounded by extractive signals or human-checked summaries, and use automatic tools to flag unsupported entities/quantities before training <cite id="107608e7-1">Training on summaries that include non-present information can increase hallucination; extrinsic hallucinations can stem from human-written summaries</cite> <cite id="48615a0b-4">A verification system for non-factual quantities plus re-ranking reduced hallucinated quantities in outputs</cite>.
- Practical pipeline: pair documents with multiple human references, compute overlap-based grounding, drop or correct misaligned spans; optionally rank reference summaries by semantic support before fine-tuning <cite id="e43d4e65-3">Overlap-based filtering of overly abstractive references yields cleaner training sets and better downstream results</cite>.

2) Add faithfulness-aware supervision signals during training
- Mine unfaithful spans and use them as negative examples: training with gradient ascent, unlikelihood training, or task vector negation on annotated unfaithful spans improves faithfulness; unlikelihood and task vector negation were most effective in ablation <cite id="48615a0b-1">Span-level hallucination annotations enable fine-tuning via gradient ascent, unlikelihood training, and task vector negation; unlikelihood and task vector negation improved faithfulness, with stable gains across weighting schedules</cite>.
- Reference-grounded fact consistency: leverage reference summaries as positives and generate erroneous summaries as negatives to train discriminators that distinguish faithful from unfaithful outputs, directly penalizing unsupported facts <cite id="48615a0b-1">Using unfaithful spans mined from reference-grounded data improves faithfulness</cite> <cite id="e43d4e65-4">Train with reference summaries as positive data and erroneous summaries as negatives to improve fact consistency</cite>.
- Entity-level verification and re-ranking: teach models to avoid hallucinated entities by incorporating entity classification/verification objectives and re-ranking steps to reduce hallucinated quantities; these auxiliary signals improve entity-level factuality without harming abstractiveness <cite id="48615a0b-4">Entity classification as auxiliary objective improves entity-level factuality; verification and re-ranking reduce hallucinated quantities in outputs</cite>.
- Reinforcement learning signals from faithfulness metrics or detectors: RL-based objectives and preference optimization can improve faithfulness, but risk overfitting to chosen signals if not balanced with generalization tasks; FactPegasus-style contrastive setups combining ROUGE and FactCC can help, yet degrade overall summarization if over-optimized <cite id="48615a0b-1">FactPegasus combines ROUGE and FactCC in contrastive pretraining to boost faithfulness, but risks overfitting to metrics</cite> <cite id="48615a0b-2">RL-based objectives have been used to enhance faithfulness; decoding strategies (ITI, DoLa, lookahead) can improve faithfulness but do not change the model’s parameters</cite>.

3) Design training data and pretraining corpora to encode faithfulness and semantic coherence
- Faithfulness-constrained pretraining: pretraining with objectives that encourage semantic coherence and faithfulness, even when training on unlabeled data, improves downstream low-shot generalization; adding explicit faithfulness constraints during pretraining yields more concise, coherent, and faithful abstractive summaries <cite id="e43d4e65-0">PELMS pretraining uses semantic coherence heuristics and faithfulness constraints over a 93M-document, 3M-cluster multi-document corpus; in low-shot multi-document summarization, it improves informativeness, abstractiveness, coherence, and faithfulness</cite>.
- Large-scale unlabeled corpora for language modeling: leveraging massive unlabeled text to pretrain encoders/decoders enhances summarization quality, but faithfulness must be explicitly enforced via semantic matching or entailment signals; otherwise models prefer abstraction that introduces unsupported content <cite id="e43d4e65-4">Pretraining encoder-decoder models on large unlabeled corpora improves generation; faithfulness requires modeling facts in the source and using faithfulness evaluation as a direct signal</cite>.
- Multi-document training sets with cluster-based diversity: topic-centric clusters provide broader coverage of entities and facts, improving the ability to abstain from unsupported content and promoting faithful fusion rather than copying <cite id="e43d4e65-0">A multi-document pre-training corpus with 93M documents and 3M topic-centric clusters supports training models that generate faithful summaries across genres</cite> <cite id="e43d4e65-1">Extending encoder-decoder to multi-document settings is challenging due to scarce labeled data; pointer-generator mechanisms copy from sources and fuse sentences</cite>.

4) Train extractive–abstractive hybrids and selectors to maintain grounded abstraction
- Copying mechanisms: pointer-generator networks explicitly copy source words/phrases, which increases faithfulness but reduces abstractiveness; careful training and selection can balance the two <cite id="e43d4e65-1">Pointer-generator networks enable copying from source text and sentence fusion; this supports moving from single- to multi-document summarization</cite> <cite id="48615a0b-2">FactPegasus modifies sentence selection by combining ROUGE with FactCC to favor grounded content over hallucinated abstractions</cite>.
- Control abstractiveness to match ground truth: models that generate more unigrams/bigrams/trigrams absent from the source increase hallucination risk; training with constraints or selecting for realistic abstractiveness levels improves fidelity to reference summaries <cite id="107608e7-2">Measuring abstractiveness as the fraction of n-grams in the summary but not the source reveals that high abstractiveness correlates with hallucinations; training can reduce this gap to approach reference levels</cite>.
- Evaluate “effective faithfulness” to separate gains from extractiveness: train selectors that enforce extractiveness-aware baselines to measure improvements that are not merely from copying more content; this reveals that many advances stem from increased extractiveness and motivates methods that raise abstraction while preserving faithfulness <cite id="e43d4e65-2">Effective faithfulness isolates faithfulness gains independent of extractiveness; analysis shows improved faithfulness often comes from higher extractiveness, motivating models that are both more abstractive and more faithful</cite>.

Practical pipelines: detecting, filtering, and selecting with faithfulness signals
- Use semantic-inference metrics (e.g., BERTScore-style, FactCC) and human-in-the-loop checks to triage training sets: models trained with such signals produce more faithful outputs than ROUGE-only training; intrinsic contradictions can be detected by fact consistency models, while extrinsic unsupported spans require semantic overlap checks <cite id="48615a0b-0">Semantic inference-based automatic measures better capture faithfulness/factuality than ROUGE/BERTScore</cite> <cite id="48615a0b-2">FactPegasus uses ROUGE+FactCC to guide contrastive pretraining; overfitting to metrics can degrade general quality</cite> <cite id="107608e7-1">Models may hallucinate by attending to irrelevant context or using noncontextual knowledge; training data with extrinsic content amplifies this</cite>.
- Build iterative selection loops: train extractive baselines to produce candidate references, filter out misaligned/overly abstractive spans, run entity/quantity verification, and re-rank summaries to reduce hallucinations before using them for abstractive fine-tuning <cite id="e43d4e65-3">Overlap-based filtering of overly abstractive references improves training sets; extractive labels derived from references can be tuned to avoid noisy supervision</cite> <cite id="48615a0b-4">Verification and re-ranking reduced hallucinated quantities in final summaries</cite>.
- Combine span-level unfaithful mining with RLHF-style preference optimization: label hallucinated spans on held-out verification sets, then fine-tune abstractive models to disfavor those patterns; this improves faithfulness without catastrophic drops in ROUGE when balanced correctly <cite id="48615a0b-1">Span-level unfaithful mining via unlikelihood training and task vector negation improves faithfulness</cite> <cite id="48615a0b-2">RL-based objectives can enhance faithfulness; decoding-time interventions alone don’t change model parameters</cite>.

Mechanisms and trade-offs to manage
- Source-grounded decoding vs. knowledge-driven abstraction: intrinsic hallucinations benefit from mechanisms that enforce semantic matching to the source; extrinsic hallucinations reflect reliance on external knowledge; retrieval-augmented training data and reference-grounded objectives mitigate both types by constraining generation to supported content <cite id="107608e7-1">Attending to irrelevant context or external knowledge contributes to hallucinations; training data content strongly influences hallucination rates</cite> <cite id="107608e7-3">Extrinsic hallucinations arise from ignoring the source; early correction is crucial</cite>.
- Abstractiveness–faithfulness trade-off: naive pursuit of ROUGE often increases abstractiveness at the cost of faithfulness; constrained pretraining, extractive copying, and extractiveness-aware selectors can raise faithfulness while approaching reference-level abstraction <cite id="48615a0b-2">FactPegasus modifies sentence selection to prefer grounded content, reducing hallucinations</cite> <cite id="107608e7-2">High abstractiveness measured by n-gram absence from the source indicates hallucinations; training can reduce abstractiveness gap to ground-truth levels</cite> <cite id="e43d4e65-2">Effective faithfulness analysis shows many faithfulness gains stem from higher extractiveness, motivating methods that improve both</cite>.
- Risks of metric overfitting and sampling: optimizing solely against faithfulness metrics or heavy use of sampling can hurt generalization or overfit to artifacts; balanced multi-objective training, diverse pretraining corpora, and robust validation with semantic inference metrics reduce these risks <cite id="48615a0b-2">Overfitting to FactCC/ROUGE can degrade overall summarization quality; RL-based objectives require careful design</cite> <cite id="48615a0b-4">High ROUGE can coexist with hallucinations, necessitating faithfulness-aware evaluation and training</cite>.

Actionable checklist: improving training data to prevent hallucinations
- Curate references: drop misaligned/overly abstractive references; prefer human-checked or extractive-grounded references; rank references by semantic support before training <cite id="e43d4e65-3">Filtering references with no bigram overlap improves training and yields better scores</cite> <cite id="107608e7-1">Training on summaries with extrinsic content increases hallucination risk</cite>.
- Add faithfulness supervision: mine unfaithful spans and include them as hard negatives; train with unlikelihood or task vector negation; build positive/negative pairs using references and generated errors <cite id="48615a0b-1">Unlikelihood and task vector negation on span-level unfaithful data improve faithfulness</cite> <cite id="e43d4e65-4">Use reference summaries as positives and erroneous summaries as negatives to train better fact consistency</cite>.
- Use entity/quantity verification: incorporate entity classification/verification and re-ranking to reduce hallucinated entities/quantities before or during fine-tuning <cite id="48615a0b-4">Entity classification plus verification and re-ranking reduced hallucinated quantities</cite>.
- Enforce grounded abstraction: add copy-based objectives and semantic coherence/entailment signals; pretrain on large, diverse corpora with faithfulness constraints; in low-resource or multi-document settings, use cluster-based pretraining to improve faithfulness at low shot <cite id="e43d4e65-0">Faithfulness-constrained pretraining on multi-document clusters improves informativeness, abstractiveness, coherence, and faithfulness at minimal fine-tuning</cite> <cite id="e43d4e65-1">Pointer-generator and MMR adaptation help extend to multi-document summarization with scarce labels</cite>.
- Balance abstractiveness: train selectors to match reference-level abstractiveness and measure effective faithfulness to ensure abstraction gains don’t come from copying more unsupported content <cite id="107608e7-2">Controlling abstractiveness to approach ground-truth reduces hallucinations</cite> <cite id="e43d4e65-2">Effective faithfulness isolates gains beyond extractiveness</cite>.
- Validate with faithfulness metrics: include semantic inference-based metrics and human evaluations in selection loops; avoid ROUGE-only optimization to prevent undetected hallucinations <cite id="48615a0b-0">Semantic inference-based measures better approximate true faithfulness than ROUGE/BERTScore</cite>.

Takeaway
- Hallucinations in abstractive summarization arise from training on noisy, misaligned, or overly abstract references and from generating unsupported content; targeted data curation, faithfulness-aware supervision, and faithfulness-constrained pretraining consistently reduce hallucinations while preserving abstractiveness when balanced with extractive grounding and entity-level verification <cite id="107608e7-1">Human-written summaries with extrinsic content bias models to hallucinate</cite> <cite id="48615a0b-1">Span-level unfaithful mining via unlikelihood and task vector negation improves faithfulness</cite> <cite id="e43d4e65-0">Faithfulness-constrained pretraining on diverse multi-document corpora yields faithful summarization without excessive fine-tuning</cite> <cite id="48615a0b-4">Entity verification and re-ranking reduce hallucinated quantities and improve entity factuality</cite>. Title: Enhancing Faithfulness in Abstractive Summarization via Span-Level Fine-Tuning
Snippet: In this study, we propose leveraging span-level hallucination annotations to improve the faithfulness of LLM-generated summaries. To this end, we construct a dataset containing organically generated summaries labeled at the span level and evaluate three fine-tuning methods-gradient ascent, unlikelihood training, and task vector negation-that leverage unfaithful summary spans. Our results show that all three approaches improve summarization faithfulness, with unlikelihood training and task vector negation being more effective. Additionally, we analyze the impact of varying the weight of negative samples (ϵ) and find that unlikelihood training remains the most stable across a wide range of values. These findings highlight the effectiveness of span-level annotations in mitigating hallucinations and offer insights into robust fine-tuning strategies for improving LLM faithfulness.

Title: Model-based Preference Optimization in Abstractive Summarization without Human Feedback
Snippet: In the realm of auto-regressive language models, there are two primary approaches aimed to enhance the model's summarization capabilities: adjusting the learning algorithm or refining the decoding strategy (Welleck et al., 2020b). The former involves updating the model's parameters through a learning objective, while the latter entails improving the decoding algorithm during generation while maintaining the existing pre-trained parameters frozen. In this paper, we will review two ap-proaches in abstractive summarization aimed at alleviating hallucination. 

Decoding Strategies Several methods have been proposed to rectify hallucinations during generation. Inference-time intervention (ITI) shifts activations along truth-correlated directions (Li et al., 2023), repeating the same intervention autoregressively until the entire answer is generated. 

Decoding by contrasting layers (DoLa) uses an early-exit strategy by contrasting the differences in logits obtained from projecting the later layers versus earlier layers (Chuang et al., 2023). Lastly, Wan et al. (2023) extend the idea of lookahead (Lu et al., 2022) to improve faithfulness in abstractive summarization, showing that the deterministic decoding strategy outperforms nucleus sampling (Holtzman et al., 2020) in terms of faithfulness. However, it is important to note that decoding strategies do not change the underlying model. 

Learning Algorithms To mitigate hallucinations, naively fine-tuning with faithfulness-aware objectives might seem straightforward. FactPegasus (Wan and Bansal, 2022) employs a tailored pretraining setup with contrastive learning to generate more faithful summaries. It modifies sentence selection by combining ROUGE and FactCC (Kryscinski et al., 2020). However, this method risks overfitting to the metrics used, potentially degrading overall summarization performance (Chae et al., 2024). 

As an alternative, RL-based objectives can be utilized to enhance faithfulness (Böhm et al., 2019;Roit et al., 2023;Paulus et al., 2018).

Snippet: We investigate pre-training techniques for abstractive multi-document summarization (MDS), which is much less studied than summarizing single documents. Though recent work has demonstrated the effectiveness of highlighting information salience for pre-training strategy design, they struggle to generate abstractive and reflective summaries, which are critical properties for MDS. To this end, we present **PELMS**, a pre-trained model that uses pre-training objectives based on semantic coherence heuristics and faithfulness constraints together with unlabeled multi-document inputs, to promote the generation of concise, fluent, and faithful summaries. To support the training of PELMS, we compile **MultiPT**, a multi-document pre-training corpus containing over 93 million documents to form more than 3million unlabeled topic-centric document clusters, covering diverse genres such as product reviews, news, and general knowledge. We perform extensive evaluation of PELMS in low-shot settings on a wide range of MDS datasets. Our approach consistently outperforms competitive comparisons with respect to overall informativeness, abstractiveness, coherence, and faithfulness, and with minimal fine-tuning can match performance of language models at a much larger scale (e.g., GPT-4).

Title: Adapting the Neural Encoder-Decoder Framework from Single to Multi-Document Summarization
Snippet: Limited by the availability of labelled data, experiments are often performed on small domain-specific datasets.

Neural abstractive summarization utilizing the encoder-decoder architecture has shown promising results but studies focus primarily on singledocument summarization (Nallapati et al., 2016;Kikuchi et al., 2016;Chen et al., 2016;Miao and Blunsom, 2016;Tan et al., 2017;Zeng et al., 2017;Zhou et al., 2017;Paulus et al., 2017;See et al., 2017;Gehrmann et al., 2018).The pointing mechanism (Gulcehre et al., 2016;Gu et al., 2016) allows a summarization system to both copy words from the source text and generate new words from the vocabulary.Reinforcement learning is exploited to directly optimize evaluation metrics (Paulus et al., 2017;Kryściński et al., 2018;Chen and Bansal, 2018).These studies fo-cus on summarizing single documents in part because the training data are abundant.

The work of Baumel et al. (2018) and Zhang et al. (2018) are related to ours.In particular, Baumel et al. (2018) propose to extend an abstractive summarization system to generate query-focused summaries; Zhang et al. (2018) add a document set encoder to their hierarchical summarization framework.With these few exceptions, little research has been dedicated to investigate the feasibility of extending the encoder-decoder framework to generate abstractive summaries from multi-document inputs, where available training data are scarce.

Title: Faithful or Extractive? On Mitigating the Faithfulness-Abstractiveness Trade-off in Abstractive Summarization
Snippet: Generating abstractive summaries of documents has been a long-standing goal of summarization. While there has been tremendous progress towards this goal (Kryściński et al., 2018;Dong et al., 2019;Zhang et al., 2019;, abstractive summarization systems still suffer from faithfulness errors (Cao et al., 2018), generating information that is not present in the original text. This has led to an increased research in faithfulness evaluation of summarization systems (Falke et al., 2019;Kryscinski et al., 2020; as * Equal contribution. Corresponding author for queries: faisal@cs.columbia.edu. well as methods to improve faithfulness of generated summaries (Kang and Hashimoto, 2020;Chen et al., 2021). Intuitively, one straightforward way of improving faithfulness of generated summaries is to copy a larger amount of content from the source article (i.e. more extraction). Thus, any methods that increase the level of extractiveness, whether intentionally or not, would improve faithfulness. Without reported extractiveness, it is unclear whether prior improvements mainly arise from increased extractiveness. We argue that in order to make progress in abstractive summarization, it is important to tease apart faithfulness improvements due to increased extractiveness versus improvements due to improved abstraction.

In order to tease this apart, we develop a framework for evaluating progress in faithfulness, by considering the effective faithfulness, i.e. the improvement in faithfulness over a baseline system (control) operating at the same level of extractiveness. Systems that improve effective faithfulness should lie above this curve.

Title: Towards Improving Faithfulness in Abstractive Summarization
Snippet: Abstractive Summarization. In recent years, the research on text generation has made impressive progress [14,15,16], which promotes the progress of abstractive summarization. The abstractive summarization task generates novel words and phrases not featured in the source text to capture the salient ideas of the source text [17]. Most works apply an encoder-decoder architecture to implicitly learn the summarization procedure [18,19]. More recently, applying pretrained language models as encoder [4,20] or pre-training the generation process by leveraging a large-scale of unlabeled corpus [21,22] brings significant improvements. Explicit structure modeling has also been shown to be effective in summarization tasks. For example, Jin et al. [23] incorporated semantic dependency graphs to help generate sentences with better semantic relevance, and Wu et al. [9] came up with a unified semantic graph to aggregate relevant disjoint context from the input. 

Fact Consistency for Abstractive Summarization. Producing a summary that is entailed by the information presented in the source document is a key challenge in the summarization task, and less progress has been made on it. Pioneer works [24,25] incorporated fact descriptions or entailment knowledge to enhance faithfulness. More recently, Zhu et al. [26] modeled the facts in the source article with knowledge graphs based on a graph neural network. Cao et al. [10] proposed to leverage reference summaries as positive training data and erroneous summaries as negative data, to train summarization systems that are better at distinguishing between them. Aralikatte et al. [27] introduced focus attention mechanism to encourage decoders to proactively generate tokens that are similar or topical to the input document. On the contrary, other works post-edit the generated summaries. Different from previous works, we enhance the semantic understanding of the document with faithfulness evaluation as a direct signal and prevent the overconfidence of LM which is not addressed before. Multi-task Learning. Multi-task learning is a learning paradigm in machine learning and it aims to leverage useful information contained in multiple related tasks to help improve the generalization performance of all the tasks [28].

Improving training data “quality” can increase hallucinations when curation removes signals that implicitly enforce faithfulness and coverage, overfits to a narrow target style, or embeds subtle corruption that models then imitate; at the same time, standard evaluation metrics can reward plausible but unsupported content. The net effect depends on what “quality” changes (noise removal vs. style/coverage), how models are trained and decoded, and how outputs are judged. <cite id="7d090d11-0">Neural abstractive summarization models frequently hallucinate, and high-ROUGE summaries can contain large amounts of hallucinatory content</cite>. <cite id="7d090d11-2">The degree of hallucination correlates with training data quality, with models trained on XSum exhibiting more factual errors than those trained on CNN/DM; removing noisy samples can reduce ROUGE and recall</cite>.

1) Noise as an implicit faithfulness regularizer
Abstractive models trained from extractive-to-abstractive setups learn to match target summaries that already blend core facts with paraphrase and omission. The presence of “noisy” but source-grounded references constrains generation to content supported by the source, even when the optimal summary would omit or paraphrase. Purifying references by removing unsupported content or by overly aggressive filtering can remove this implicit supervision, letting models extrapolate farther from the source to maximize density/fluency under weak attribution signals. <cite id="7d090d11-2">The degree of hallucinations correlates with training data quality; models trained on XSum have more factual errors than those on CNN/DM; removing noisy samples reduces ROUGE and entity recall, indicating that filtered data loses useful task-specific knowledge</cite>. <cite id="aa9bd967-4">An analysis links hallucinations to training on target summaries unsupported by the source, and proposes decoding constraints to avoid such unsupported content</cite>. <cite id="aa9bd967-1">Using clean and noisy data jointly via contrastive parameter ensembling reduces hallucinations without sacrificing ROUGE or information recall, underscoring that variation in noise provides signals to avoid unsupported content</cite>.

When training corpora are curated for high lexical overlap or stylistic fluency (e.g., high-ROUGE references), models optimize for producing plausible, fluent summaries that mirror those references, which can privilege style-driven abstraction over faithful content selection. Improving data quality often increases ROUGE-1/2/L of references (e.g., standardized, cleaned, back-translated references). Why Improving Data Quality Can Backfire
- Removing the “messy middle” of training data: Abstractive training benefits from references that reflect real trade-offs between inclusion, paraphrase, and omission. Combine lexical filtering with coverage/faithfulness objectives to prevent recall collapse and style-driven hallucination. <cite id="aa9bd967-0">Entity precision filtering on XSum reduces ROUGE and entity recall, showing that aggressive filters harm coverage</cite>. <cite id="aa9bd967-4">PINOCCHIO improves consistency by 67% at decoding time by constraining beam search to avoid unsupported content</cite>.
- Inspect curated data provenance: Audit references for contamination, number/date inconsistencies, and back-translation errors; prefer verifiable sources and entity-level truth checks. Use entity-level factuality signals during training and re-ranking. <cite id="aa9bd967-3">Entity-level verification and re-ranking reduce non-factual quantities in outputs; summary-worthiness tasks improve entity-level factuality</cite>.
- Use better evaluators: Prefer human judgments and factual metrics over ROUGE alone; adopt semantic inference metrics and adversarial probes to detect hallucinations not visible to ROUGE. <cite id="7d090d11-0">High ROUGE can coexist with hallucinations, motivating improved evaluation</cite>. <cite id="7d090d11-1">Semantic inference-based automatic measures better capture faithfulness than ROUGE or BERTScore</cite>.
- Leverage noisy data constructively: Instead of discarding noisy samples, train dual pathways (clean vs. noisy) and combine parameters to counteract hallucinations while retaining fluency, as in contrastive parameter ensembling. <cite id="aa9bd967-1">Clean/noisy fine-tuning yields expert/antiexpert parameters; parameter adjustment reduces hallucinations without significant ROUGE loss</cite>.

Improving training data quality can increase hallucinations when curation removes implicit faithfulness signals, overoptimizes for fluent stylization, or embeds silent factual errors that models then imitate; at the same time, standard metrics can reward plausible but unsupported content. The key is to maintain a training signal that ties outputs to the source (via noisy/coverage-rich supervision or explicit factuality objectives), preserve diverse coverage, and evaluate with human and factual metrics rather than ROUGE alone. <cite id="7d090d11-0">Hallucinations are common and can be high-ROUGE</cite>; <cite id="7d090d11-2">training data quality correlates with hallucination severity</cite>; <cite id="aa9bd967-0">filtering can reduce ROUGE and recall</cite>; and <cite id="aa9bd967-2">leveraging clean/noisy variation reduces hallucinations without sacrificing informativeness</cite>.

Snippet: Hallucination is a known issue for neural abstractive summarization models. Recent work suggests that the degree of hallucination may depend on errors in the training data. We first select clean and noisy subsets from the training data using different automatic factual metrics. Then, we fine-tune a base summarization model, which is trained on all training samples, on the clean (noisy) subset to obtain an \textit{expert} (\textit{anti-expert}) model. Finally, we adjust the parameters of base model by the difference between parameters of the \textit{expert} and \textit{anti-expert} models, steering the base model towards the \textit{expert} model and away from the \textit{anti-expert} model. Title: CaPE: Contrastive Parameter Ensembling for Reducing Hallucination in Abstractive Summarization

Title: Hallucinated but Factual! Inspecting the Factuality of Hallucinations in Abstractive Summarization
Snippet: Maynez et al. (2020) conducted a large-scale human evaluation of several neural abstractive summarization systems, and found that hallucinations are common among the outputs of different summarization models.

Recently, many methods have been proposed to reduce model hallucination. Kang and Hashimoto (2020) propose a "loss truncation" training algorithm that filters out noisy training samples which may lead a model to hallucinate.  use a verification system to recognize non-factual quantities in summaries and adopt a re-ranking system to reduce the number of hallucinated quantities in the final output summary. Narayan et al. (2021) use entity chains to mitigate the hallucination problem in the generation of abstractive summaries. Nan et al. (2021) show that data filtering and use a summary-worthy entity classification task as an auxiliary training objective can help improve model's entity-level factuality.

Filippova (2020) proposed a method for controlling hallucination in data-to-text generation task. They suggest that a conditional language model (CLM) will put more probability mass on a nonhallucinated entity than an unconditional language model (LM). Our work differs in that we focus on both hallucination and factuality. Also, our method works at the entity-level rather than the sentencelevel, and is geared towards text summarization.

Title: CaPE: Contrastive Parameter Ensembling for Reducing Hallucination in Abstractive Summarization
Snippet: Neural abstractive summarization systems have been shown to generate plausible summaries with high lexical overlap with the references. However, human analyses (Fabbri et al., 2021a;Pagnoni et al., 2021;Tejaswin et al., 2021) and automatic evaluations (Falke et al., 2019;Kryscinski et al., 2020;Maynez et al., 2020;Durmus et al., 2020) show that state-of-the-art models trained on the widely used XSUM (Narayan et al., 2018) and CNN/DM (Hermann et al., 2015)   information with high frequency. The degree of a model's hallucinations further correlates with the quality of the training data (Aralikatte et al., 2021;Pagnoni et al., 2021). For instance, models trained on the XSum data tend to generate a higher proportion of factual errors as compared to models trained on the CNN/DM dataset. 

Given the association between training data quality and hallucinations in resulting models, the easiest method to reduce hallucinations is to remove noisy samples from the training data (Nan et al., 2021). However, data filtering reduces the size of training data and consequently, the diversity in target summary since the removed noisy samples might also include useful task-specific knowledge. This impacts other aspects of the generated summaries such as information recall or fluency. In Table 1, we show ROUGE (R-1/2/L) and named entity recall (E-R ref ) with respect to the reference summary of a BART model (Lewis et al., 2020) trained on the entity precision-filtered XSUM data (24.6% of the original data). The new model drops 8-18% in ROUGE and 20% drop in entity recall. 

In this work, we design a simple yet effective strategy to utilize both clean and noisy training samples.

Title: Reducing named entity hallucination risk to ensure faithful summary generation
Snippet: The faithfulness of abstractive text summarization at the named entities level is the focus of this study. We propose to add a new criterion to the summary selection method based on the “risk” of generating entities that do not belong to the source document. This method is based on the assumption that Out-Of-Document entities are more likely to be hallucinations. This assumption was verified by a manual annotation of the entities occurring in a set of generated summaries on the CNN/DM corpus. This study showed that only 29% of the entities outside the source document were inferrable by the annotators, leading to 71% of hallucinations among OOD entities. We test our selection method on the CNN/DM corpus and show that it significantly reduces the hallucination risk on named entities while maintaining competitive results with respect to automatic evaluation metrics like ROUGE.

Title: Improving the Faithfulness of Abstractive Summarization via Entity Coverage Control
Snippet: In this paper, we propose ECC to address extrinsic hallucination in abstractive summarization in both supervised and zero-shot settings. Our extensive experiments demonstrate that the proposed method effectively reduces entity hallucination without hurting the quality of the generated summaries.

Title: Optum at MEDIQA 2021: Abstractive Summarization of Radiology Reports using simple BART Finetuning
Snippet: Our proposed method leverages pretrained summarization models. We finetuned three types of pretrained models for the radiology report summarization; BART (Lewis et al., 2019), T5 (Raffel et al., 2020) and Pegasus (Zhang et al., 2020a). We used Huggingface Transformers (Wolf et al., 2020) library for finetuning. 

BART: Developed by Facebook, BART is a denoising autoencoder. Since it uses the standard transformer-based neural machine translation architecture, it is a generalization of both BERT and GPT3 (Brown et al., 2020). For pretraining, it was trained by shuffling the order of sentence (an extension of next sentence prediction) and text infilling (an extension of the language masking).
